summary: This informational document describes how the China Education and Research Network designed and deployed IVI, a stateless mapping between IPv4 and IPv6 addresses. IVI lets IPv6-only networks talk to the IPv4 Internet and the other way around, using subsets of an ISP's IPv4 addresses. It is a deployment report.

plainLanguage.summary: Some computers speak an old address language and some a new one. IVI is a translator that follows fixed rules, and this describes a university network setting one up.

questions: how does ivi map ipv4 to ipv6
subtitle: How a Chinese research network let IPv6-only hosts and the IPv4 Internet reach each other with a stateless address mapping.

tldr.problem: CERNET is IPv4-only and CERNET2 is IPv6-only, yet hosts on the IPv6 side needed to talk to the IPv4 Internet. Dual stack, tunnels and NAT-PT did not solve that cleanly.
tldr.mechanism: IVI embeds a subset of an ISP's IPv4 addresses inside the ISP's own IPv6 prefix with a fixed, stateless rule. Translators between the two networks rewrite headers using SIIT and keep no per-connection state.
tldr.outcome: IVI was an early design deployed in CERNET as a reference for the IETF standards on IPv4/IPv6 stateless translation. The RFC points to RFC 6052, RFC 6145, RFC 6146 and RFC 6147 as the IETF standard mechanisms.

facts.label: Embedded IPv4 bits
facts.value: Bits 40 to 71 of the IPv6 address

facts.label: Extra IPv6 size
facts.value: At least 20 bytes larger than IPv4

today: RFC 6219 is an Informational document with no obsoleting or updating RFCs listed. It describes an early design, and the text itself points to RFC 6052, RFC 6145, RFC 6146 and RFC 6147 as the IETF standard translation mechanisms.

sections.title: Why Translation Was Needed
sections.content:
RFC 6219 describes the IVI translation design that the China Education and Research Network (CERNET) built and deployed. In Roman numerals IV is 4 and VI is 6, so IVI stands for IPv4/IPv6 translation. CERNET has two backbones: CERNET is IPv4-only and CERNET2 is IPv6-only.

The document argues that existing options fall short. Dual-stack hosts can talk to both families, but single-stack hosts can only talk within their own. Tunnels link IPv6 islands across IPv4 networks but cannot connect the two families. NAT-PT was reclassified from Proposed Standard to Historic, and the RFC lists its problems: it breaks protocols that embed addresses in payloads, loses end-to-end address transparency, and keeps state in the translator.

From this the RFC sets six requirements: support IPv6-initiated and IPv4-initiated communication, avoid growing the global routing tables, allow incremental deployment, use IPv4 addresses effectively, be stateless for scalability, and keep DNS decoupled from the translator.
sections.plainLanguage: Some computers only understand the old address language and some only the new one. Earlier tricks were clumsy, so the authors built a cleaner translator.

sections.title: The IVI Address Mapping
sections.content:
IVI is a prefix-specific and stateless mapping. Inside an ISP's IPv6 block, usually a /32, a small portion is the image of the whole global IPv4 space. IPv6 hosts use a subset of the ISP's own IPv4 addresses, mapped into that IPv6 space, so they can reach the global IPv6 Internet directly and the IPv4 Internet through stateless translators.

In the CERNET implementation, bits 0 to 31 are the ISP's /32 prefix, bits 32 to 39 are all ones as an identifier of IVI addresses, and bits 40 to 71 carry the embedded IPv4 address. Based on this rule an IPv4 /24 maps to an IPv6 /64 and an IPv4 /32 maps to an IPv6 /72. The example prefix is 2001:db8:ff00::/40.

The RFC notes that the IETF standard address format is defined in RFC 6052.
sections.plainLanguage: Every old-style address gets a new-style twin built by tucking it into a longer address. Because the rule never changes, anyone can work out the twin without asking.

sections.title: Routing and the Translator
sections.content:
The IVI translator is a special dual-stack router with one interface in the IPv4 network and one in the IPv6 network. A single interface with both address types is also possible. Router R1 on the IPv4 side routes the IVI4 range to the translator, and router R2 on the IPv6 side routes the IVIG6 /40 to it. The routes can be static or learned through IGP or BGP.

Because IVI4(i) and IVI6(i) aggregate into the ISP's own IPv4 and IPv6 blocks at its border routers, they do not affect the global routing tables. Translation is stateless, so the same prefix can be used on several translators for multihoming. Each ISP can deploy it independently, which allows incremental deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: The translator sits at the border gate between the two towns. Since it keeps no notes, you can put several gates in the same place and any of them will do.

sections.title: Translating Headers, ICMP and Applications
sections.content:
Network-layer header translation MUST follow SIIT (RFC 2765) except for the source and destination addresses, which use the IVI mapping. For example, Type of Service becomes Traffic Class, TTL becomes Hop Limit, and the IPv4 Header Checksum is discarded. In the other direction the IPv4 header gets IHL = 5 and a recalculated checksum.

Transport-layer checksums for TCP and UDP include the IP header, so they MUST be recalculated. IPv6 packets end up at least 20 bytes larger than IPv4 ones, so MTU and fragmentation handling follow SIIT too. For ICMP, the current prototype uses a small IPv4 address block to stand in for IPv6 addresses outside IVIG6, so translated ICMP messages are not dropped as coming from unknown or private sources.

Most applications such as HTTP, SSH and Telnet work. Applications that use IP addresses to identify peers, such as FTP, need an Application Layer Gateway (ALG), which can be integrated into the translator. The RFC says RFC 6145 contains the updated IETF specification for header, ICMP and fragmentation translation.
sections.plainLanguage: When a letter crosses the border, the translator rewrites the address label and fixes the stamp. A few special letters that mention addresses inside need a helper.

sections.title: DNS, Multicast and Host Setup
sections.content:
DNS is decoupled from the translator. For IVI6 hosts, each name has both an A record and an AAAA record. For IPv4-only names, an IVI DNS server, which MUST be deployed in a dual-stack environment, looks for an AAAA record first. If none exists it fetches the A record, maps it into IVIG6 and returns a synthesized AAAA record. The RFC defers the technical specification to RFC 6147.

IVI can also carry PIM-SSM multicast. IPv4 232.0.0.0/8 maps to IPv6 ff3e:0:0:0:0:0:f000:0000/96, and the IPv6 source MUST be an IVI6 address so that Reverse Path Forwarding works with PIM-SM.

IVI6 addresses have a special format, so stateless autoconfiguration cannot be used. Hosts get them by manual configuration or stateful DHCPv6. Because a host may hold several addresses, it should use an IVI6 address to reach IPv4 networks; the short-term workaround is to make it the default source address.
sections.plainLanguage: A phone book that only lists new-style addresses gets a helper. If a name has no new-style address, the helper looks up the old one and converts it. Hosts have to be told their address, because it cannot be guessed.

sections.title: Implementation, Testing and Security
sections.content:
An IVI implementation exists for Linux. The translator has been deployed between CERNET (IPv4-only) and CNGI-CERNET2 (IPv6-only) since March 2006. Pure-IPv6 web servers with IVI6 addresses behind it can be reached by IPv4 hosts, and IPv6 clients behind it can reach IPv4 servers. Both manual and DHCPv6 address configuration were tested with success.

On security, the RFC leaves general IPv4 and IPv6 issues to other documents and calls out three: IPsec and its NAT traversal, DNSSEC and firewall rules. Because IVI keeps end-to-end address transparency, IPsec could work with or without NAT traversal. DNSSEC validation is terminated at the IVI DNS for the A-to-AAAA translation. Firewall rules can be written in either family, though routers that only support access lists or uRPF for prefixes shorter than /64 may constrain this. The authors report no special security problems from their experiments.
sections.plainLanguage: The translator has been running at a real university network for years. The main worry is that some safety rules and checks need extra care when addresses are rewritten.
